blocks.text: [II, 848] ἀρθῆναι δὲ, καὶ εἰς βαθὺν ἀέρα μετεωρισθῆναι φύσιν οὐκ ἔχει. θεῖ δὲ ὤκιστα, καὶ τὰς παρὰ τὴν πλευρὰν ἑκατέραν πτέρυγας ἁπλοῖ, καὶ ἐμπῖπτον τὸ πνεῦμα κολποῖ, δίκην ἱστίων αὐτάς. [arthēnai de, kai eis bathyn aera meteōristhēnai physin ouk echei. thei de ōkista, kai tas para tēn pleuran hekateran pterygas haploi, kai empipton to pneuma kolpoi, dikēn histiōn autas.] The ostrich is indeed furnished with dense wings. Yet its nature does not allow it to be lifted from the ground by them and borne aloft. But it runs as swiftly as possible and spreads out its wings on either side, and the wind fills them like sails. And in book 4, chapter 37: Εἰ δὲ αὐτὴν διώκοι τις, ἥδε οὐκ ἐπιτολμᾷ τῇ πτήσει, θεῖ δὲ τὰς πτέρυγας ἁπλώσασα· [Ei de autēn diōkoi tis, hēde ouk epitolma tē ptēsei, thei de tas pterygas haplōsasa;] If anyone pursues it, it does not attempt to fly, but runs with its wings spread out. And in book 8, chapter 10, the same author relates that elephants in battle spread out their wide ears δίκην τῶν στρουθῶν τῶν μεγάλων, ἅπερ οὖν τὰς πτέρυγας ἁπλώσασαι, ἢ φεύγουσιν, ἢ ἐπιᾶσιν [dikēn tōn strouthōn tōn megalōn, haper oun tas pterygas haplōsasai, ē pheugousin, ē epiasin], in the manner of ostriches, which, whether they flee or attack, move with wings spread out. Philes, chapter 3:
Κολποῦν ἑαυτῆς τὰ πτερὰ πρὸς τὸν δρόμον, ῾Ως λαῖφος οἰδοῦν ἐκ πνοῆς πλησιστίου· [Kolpoun heautēs ta ptera pros ton dromon, Hōs laiphos oidoun ek pnoēs plēsistiou;]

Spreading its wings for running, like a sail swelling with the wind that fills it. Hence Pliny, book 10, chapter 20: they surpass the speed (of a horseman), their wings having been given them only for this, to help them as they run. And Claudian, Against Eutropius, book 2:
As the huge bird of Libya, when pressed by the cries of hunters, crosses the hot sands at a run, and, its wings curved by the blast like a sail, flies amid the dust. —

He says both run and fly, because the gait of the ostrich in flight is something between running and flying, or a mixture of the two. To this belong these words of Plautus in the Persa, Act 2, Scene 2:
Fly at a run. P. That is what the sea-sparrow usually does around the circus. [col. 246]
